rss.title: The War Against Slop and an Emerging Weapon to Fight it: Formal Verification
rss.summary: Proving software correct with math has traditionally required specialist work. Now AI and Lean are helping automate the process.
rss.text_excerpt:
The word of the year in the AI industry over 2026 has been “slop” — meaning low-quality output from a large language model. And with so much code being AI-generated now, avoiding slop has become a daily concern for software engineers. So how to do that? One way is to use formal verification systems , which use mathematical proofs and logic to verify the correctness of software or hardware. How formal verification is used in software and AI today In order to better understand the landscape of formal verification systems, we spoke to one of its leading proponents: Clark Barrett , &Truth’s co-founder and co-CEO. He’s also Corbel Professor (Research) of Computer Science at Stanford and was the co-creator of cvc5 , a popular automated reasoning engine used in formal verification. Without getting too in the weeds, cvc5 is what’s called a “solver” for satisfiability modulo theories (SMT) , which Barrett says is widely used in companies like Amazon. For instance, cvc5 is used for specification analysis and test generation in Kiro , Amazon’s agentic development environment. “It's been fun to see my tools go from a good idea in the lab to cvc5 is now called billions of times a day in production pipelines at Amazon,” Barrett told us. When AI coding agent companies talk about “verifying” their work, it typically means agents running tests, critiquing their own output, or having another AI model judge it. So I asked Barrett how far short of real verification does that fall? “The main difference is really just, how do you know when you're done,” he replied. “So if you're testing, patching, scanning — using all these existing tools — they're quite good. I mean, they find a ton of problems. They raise those issues. The company combines AI with automated reasoning techniques to construct proofs that Lean can check. rss.title: Combatting adversarial distillation
rss.summary: OpenAI’s layered approach to adversarial distillation combines model training, safeguards, detection, and enforcement to protect against capability extraction.
rss.text_excerpt:
As frontier AI models become more capable, safeguards play an increasingly important role in how they can be used responsibly. Adversarial distillation creates a path for bad actors to reproduce these capabilities without appropriate safeguards. An actor may use a frontier model’s outputs without authorization to train another model with similar capabilities, then deploy it without comparable protections. For instance, an adversary might distill a model’s cyber capabilities and use the resulting model to help carry out cyberattacks that the original model would have refused to assist with or that its safeguards would have blocked. We’re sharing how OpenAI detects and disrupts adversarial distillation, how we’ve strengthened protections for our models’ protected reasoning, and what we’ve learned that can help strengthen defenses across the industry. Our approach to adversarial distillation combines adversarial testing, model training, classifiers, and API-level protections with investigations into coordinated attempts to extract model capabilities. These updated safeguards align more closely with those we use for biology and cybersecurity. We place particular emphasis on preventing attackers from extracting our models’ protected reasoning: the intermediate steps a model generates internally while working toward an answer, known as its chain-of-thought. These traces can contain information the final answer leaves out, making them especially valuable training data for another model. W e’ve strengthened our defenses against protected reasoning extraction in GPT‑6.2 Astra and GPT‑6.2 Sol. In an internal adaptive evaluation using strong automated red-teaming , we tested whether attackers could recover protected reasoning the model had generated while answering an earlier prompt. The average attack success rate fell from 54.0% against GPT‑6 Astra with its original safeguards to 0.2% against GPT‑6.2 Astra with its updated safeguards. Distillation is a common machine-learning technique in which one model learns from data produced by another. For example, a model can learn from another model’s answers, its reasoning, or its judgments about which answers are better and why . rss.title: Can AI help scientists identify promising drug candidates?
rss.summary: MedChemBench evaluates how well AI models interpret molecular structures, reason from experimental evidence, and select compounds in early drug discovery.
rss.text_excerpt:
We’re introducing MedChemBench, a benchmark that evaluates AI models on reasoning tasks drawn from medicinal chemistry research. It tests whether models can connect a molecule’s structure with experimental evidence to explain results, compare compounds, and predict their properties. Building AI that can reliably support this work is one step towards helping scientists develop better medicines. One of the hardest parts of this work is that improving one property of a molecule can make another worse. A compound might act strongly against a disease related protein but be poorly absorbed or break down too quickly in the body. Medicinal chemists work through these tradeoffs by designing, making, and testing related compounds, then deciding what to try next. For AI to help, it needs to connect changes in molecular structure with experimental evidence and reason about what compounds are worth pursuing. MedChemBench measures these abilities through 99 problems drawn from published research. At the xhigh reasoning setting, GPT‑6.2 Astra earned 84.5% of the available credit, compared with 83.3% for GPT‑6 Astra, 82.0% for GPT‑6.1 Sol, and 58.2% for GPT‑5.6 Sol. GPT‑6 Astra was strongest at reconstructing molecular structures and explaining experimental evidence. Selecting compounds and predicting their numerical properties proved harder for that model. MedChemBench draws on 117 papers and patents and includes 761 distinct molecular structures. For most problems, models receive the context available at a chosen point in a research program: the biological target, the researchers’ goals, the compounds studied so far, and selected experimental findings. The benchmark evaluates four components: Molecular structures. Correct atom connections and specified stereochemistry in molecules assembled from the drawings and chemical groups provided. Scientific reasoning. Explanations supported by the supplied evidence, such as the reasons for choosing one compound over another. Ranking and selection. Compound rankings and choices that meet the stated requirements. Property predictions. Agreement with the numerical values and categories reported in the source material, including measured and calculated molecular properties. Linear was founded to build a better issue tracker. Seven years and $134 million in funding later, its CEO Karri Saarinen published a post titled "Issue tracking is dead." In this episode, we chat with Cristina Cordova , COO of Linear , about how the company navigated that and how its go-to-market changed along the way. Cristina spent seven and a half years at Stripe, led platform and partnerships at Notion, and was a partner at First Round before joining Linear in 2023. Linear's founders built it after living with legacy issue trackers at Coinbase, Airbnb and Uber, and it spread self-serve through startups like Vercel and Ramp. When she joined, Linear had about 40 people and one salesperson. Since then it has shipped an MCP server, a platform for building agents into Linear, integrations with Codex, Cursor and GitHub Copilot, and its own Linear Agent. rss.title: PostgreSQL 19 Released
rss.summary: PostgreSQL 19 Released Most years PostgreSQL ships a new release in September, but this year's release came two months later thanks mainly to the flurry of issues that the PostgreSQL team needed to address as part of the ongoing AI-reported vulnerability apocalypse. This release was definitely worth the wait. My favorite new feature is this one: For applications that send reads to standbys, PostgreSQL 19 adds "read-your-writes" consistency with the new WAIT FOR LSN command. A session on a standby can use WAIT FOR LSN to wait until the standby has replayed the write-ahead log (WAL) up to a specific log sequence number (LSN) before running a query, so the application can read data it just wrote on the primary. In practice, that looks like this: UPDATE movie SET genre = 'Dramatic' WHERE genre = 'Drama'; SELECT pg_current_wal_insert_lsn(); That returns a value like 0/0306EE20 . Store that somewhere (a signed cookie would work) such that on a subsequent request your application can do: WAIT FOR LSN '0/0306EE20' WITH (TIMEOUT '0.1s'); SELECT * FROM movie WHERE genre = 'Drama'; The timeout is optional - if you provide one you'll get an error if the replica you are talking to doesn't catch up within the specified time. I first encountered this pattern in Wikipedia , which has a hand-rolled version of this built against MySQL replication: In addition to this, MediaWiki attempts to ensure that the user sees events occurring on the wiki in chronological order. A few seconds of lag can be tolerated, as long as the user sees a consistent picture from subsequent requests. This is done by saving the primary binlog position in the session, and then at the start of each request, waiting for the replica to catch up to that position before doing any reads from it. Here's the relevant MediaWiki code , which these days uses MySQL's WAIT_FOR_EXECUTED_GTID_SET() function and falls back to SOURCE_POS_WAIT() . The staggering pace of agentic development has made traditional approaches to performance engineering unsustainable. To keep up, we built the Performance Factory, an autonomous system that uses the full capabilities of Codex and our models to find and fix regressions at an unprecedented speed. The Performance Factory, which runs in the cloud and automates investigating and resolving performance problems, enables us to keep pace with the ambition of our roadmap. In the Performance Factory, our engineers define workflows for recurring jobs and write instructions for the Codex agents that carry them out. In particular, the Regression Workflow opens a task when a performance alert fires. An agent investigates the slowdown, records its findings in the task, and proposes a fix for an engineer to review. After deployment, another agent picks up the same task to check whether performance has returned to baseline. From investigating to authoring the fix to verifying mitigation, this first workflow in the Performance Factory has automated the entire process of fixing regressions. In just over three months, the Regression Workflow tracked more than 1,700 investigations and root caused over 600 cases. That’s 17 automated investigations every day. Here, we’ll share how our use of Codex evolved into what’s now the Performance Factory, walk through our first running workflow, and share early lessons from building and running agent workflows in production. As we used Codex for more of our performance work, we noticed a progression in how our team worked. We hope other service teams can learn from our process as they adopt agentic workflows in other domains. 1. Pre-Codex . rss.title: How Public Evals Are Built Today and What Should Change
rss.summary: Patterns, gaps, and hot takes from studying 12 agent benchmarks.
rss.text_excerpt:
As models ship faster, eval scores are often the first thing we learn about a new model. But how much weight should we put in them? In eight of twelve public evals studied, there’s evidence the grader failed work that should have passed. And even when the grader gets it right, many benchmarks measure what’s easy rather than what matters, and should instead focus on reliability, work velocity, multi-turn collaboration, etc. Here, we’ll cover the common patterns and principles, the errors models make, and where current benchmarks fall short. I’ll also share what we’re getting wrong and what should change, including why average pass rate isn’t enough and why dollars are the wrong measure of cost. Finally, we’ll walk through twelve evals: four on coding and science, six on knowledge work, and two on browsing and computer use. By the end, you’ll know what to trust in a benchmark and what to question. Patterns: How eval tasks are built and maintained # Most eval tasks share four components: Instruction: A prompt that sounds like a real user’s request. The agent gets it once at the start and typically can’t ask clarifying questions. Environment: The workspace where the agent operates. Typically comes with the files, software, and services needed. For coding, this is usually a container with a repo at a specific git commit. For knowledge work, it might be a VM with installed software, simulated business apps, or a folder of documents. Grader: This decides whether the work passes. It can be deterministic code (tests and assertions over the final output or environment state), an LLM judge scoring a rubric of yes/no criteria, or a mix of both. Reference (optional): A human expert’s solution. Evals include this to prove a task is solvable, anchor pairwise comparisons, or establish a human baseline. Strands Box

An open source sandbox engine for AI agents.

## Overview Strands Box is an open source sandbox for AI agents. It combines operating-system isolation with semantic policies written in [Dogwood](https://dogwood-policy.github.io/dogwood/), so you can control what agents can access and the conditions under which they can act. Box is harness-agnostic. You choose the agent program or binary to run, configure its access in `box.toml`, and write its policies in `policy.dw`. The host OS enforces the direct access restrictions in `box.toml`. Strands Shell, Monty for Python, the egress gateway, and the MCP broker send the operations they handle to the embedded Dogwood Local Engine, which evaluates the rules in `policy.dw`. Box enforces its allow or deny decisions outside the agent process. Dogwood uses `permit` and `forbid` rules. Operations checked by the engine are denied by default: a matching `permit` must allow the operation, and a matching `forbid` overrides that permission. Box's interpreters and gateways share an event history, so rules can use earlier actions and elapsed time to decide what is allowed next. For example, a file read through Shell or Python can cause the gateway to deny a later outbound HTTP request. **Preview:** Box supports local execution on Linux ARM64, Linux x86-64, and macOS with Apple silicon. # Stately Agent **Make invalid agent actions impossible.** Agent logic as state machines: deterministic, inspectable, resumable, runs anywhere. The machine owns control flow; the model only ever picks a legal event. What you get: - **Proofs with no model.** Put the rule that must never break behind a sentinel state, then `canReach(machine, "refundedOverLimit", options)` returns `reachable: false` and `complete: true` with no API key. See [Testing and verification](https://github.com/statelyai/agent/blob/next/docs/verify.md). - **Resume and replay from the event log.** A paused run resumes with `runAgent(machine, { snapshot, event })`, and `replay(machine, result.events)` rebuilds any point of a run with no model calls. See [The event log](https://github.com/statelyai/agent/blob/next/docs/event-log.md). - **Checked ports.** `checkParity` records the old code's side effects, replays them against the machine, and reports every scenario where the two differ. `compareRuns` labels outcome-level differences `same`, `intended`, or `regression`. See [Parity with the code you replace](https://github.com/statelyai/agent/blob/next/docs/evals.md#parity-with-the-code-you-replace). The machine is also a diagram: stream any run to the Stately inspector with `runAgent`'s `inspect` option. See [Inspect a run](https://github.com/statelyai/agent/blob/next/docs/observability.md#inspect-a-run). # Paxeer X Network Paxeer X Network is a distributed HyperState Machine for payments, code execution and intent routing, developed by Sidiora Labs. The LayerX kernel is the core of the network and runs inside every `paxd` node. It executes each transaction when it arrives, assigns the next position in one global sequence and returns a signed execution receipt before any block is voted. It builds every block: the proposed block is the sealed sequence, with the signed sequence batch first and the executed transactions behind it in sequence order. Validators check that batch and the pinned proposer, replay the block and commit it; they do not select or order transactions. `paxd` uses EVM chain identifier **125** (`0x7d`) and native token **PAX**. What runs on the kernel: - [Native payments](modules/layerxpay/) with escrow, budgets, streams and services. - [Spot](modules/spot/) and [perpetual markets](modules/perps/). - [Rust programs](programs/). - [Agents](modules/layerxagent/) with delegated authority and the [pooled inference market](programs/crates/layerx-programs-ai-market/). - [Sub-chains](modules/layerxchains/) as tenant domains of the same sequence. - [The EVM](modules/evm/) with its native precompiles. - [The bridge](modules/layerxbridge/). ## Repository layout | Directory | Holds | Page | | --- | --- | --- | | [`admin/`](admin/README.md) | Node administration tools and commands. | [README](admin/README.md) | | [`api/`](api/README.md) | Protobuf API definitions and generated interfaces. | [README](api/README.md) | | [`apps/`](apps/README.md) | User-facing Paxeer applications. | [README](apps/README.md) | | [`cmd/`](cmd/README.md) | Paxeer command-line tools. | [README](cmd/README.md) | | [`consensus/`](consensus/README.md) | The network consensus engine. | [README](consensus/README.md) | | [`contracts/`](contracts/README.md) | On-chain contracts and contract tests. | [README](contracts/README.md) | | [`core/`](core/README.md) | Pinned core dependencies. | [README](core/README.md) | | [`custodyproof/`](custodyproof/README.md) | Custody proof types and verification. | [README](custodyproof/README.md) | | [`daemon/`](daemon/README.md) | The `paxd` daemon and node entry point. | [README](daemon/README.md) | | [`deploy/`](deploy/README.md) | Deployment configuration and manifests. | [README](deploy/README.md) | | [`docker/`](docker/README.md) | Docker image

screen-relay starts a desktop on a Linux VM, sandbox, or container, or attaches to the display of a Mac or the signed-in desktop of a Windows PC, and streams it to a browser as H.264. An agent controls the same desktop one command at a time: it takes a screenshot, clicks or types, and takes another screenshot to check the result. The `screen-relay` CLI, a Node SDK, and an HTTP and WebSocket API all reach the same session. ## Install ```bash npm install -g screen-relay screen-relay install # system packages and the engine build (first time only) ``` - **Requirements:** Node 22 or newer. On Linux: Debian, Ubuntu, Fedora, Arch Linux, or Alpine. On macOS: Homebrew and the Xcode Command Line Tools. On Windows: Windows 10 or later on x64, with a user signed in at the PC's screen. - **Scripts and agents:** `screen-relay install --yes` skips the confirmation. At a terminal, `install` asks before it installs packages. - **Wayland:** `screen-relay install --backend wayland`. The default backend on Linux is X11. - **Client only:** the npm install alone is enough to control a session on another machine. Requirements, backends, and Windows are covered in [Getting started](https://screen-relay.dev/docs/getting-started). ## Quick start ```bash screen-relay up -d # start a display, a desktop, and the engine screen-relay run -- xfce4-terminal # open an app on the desktop screen-relay screenshot screen.png # see the screen screen-relay click 0.5 0.5 # coordinates are fractions of the screen screen-relay type "echo hello" screen-relay key Enter screen-relay down ``` - `up` prints a viewer link. github.text_excerpt: # NimCap 截图工具 · 离线 AI，让截图继续发挥作用 **简体中文** | [English](README.en.md) [GitHub](https://github.com/nimcap/nimcap-screenshot) · [Gitee 镜像（旧仓库名）](https://gitee.com/lilongjiang/SnapSharp) · [官方网站](https://jietu.nimcap.com/) · [下载发布版](https://github.com/nimcap/nimcap-screenshot/releases) NimCap 截图工具（NimCap Screenshot）是一款面向 Windows 的开源桌面工具，把**截图、标注、贴图、长截图和录屏**，与**本地 OCR、翻译、表格与公式识别、抠图、去水印及图像修复**放在同一个工作流程中。从屏幕取一张图，既可以直接分享，也可以继续提取文字、整理表格、生成 LaTeX、移除背景，或将参考资料贴在桌面。 **离线 AI 是它的核心能力：图片和文字在本机处理，无需上传云端完成本地识别、翻译与图像处理。** 提前准备好程序、对应模型和运行依赖后，这些功能可在断网电脑或无互联网连接的内网中使用，适合整理内部资料、制作教程、阅读外文文档和日常办公。基础截图、标注、贴图、取色、测量与条码解码无需下载 AI 模型。 项目属于 `nimcap`，原名 SnapSharp，当前 GitHub 主仓库为 `nimcap/nimcap-screenshot`；Gitee 作为镜像入口保留旧仓库名。软件使用 C#、WPF 和 .NET 10 构建，面向 Windows x64，通过系统托盘和全局快捷键调用。旧版升级与数据目录选择见[迁移说明](#upgrade)。 ## 离线 AI 可以做什么 | 需要完成的工作 | 本机处理方式 | 得到的结果 | |---|---|---| | 把截图变成文字 | PaddleOCR；也可选择 Windows OCR 或 Tesseract | 可编辑文字、复制或导出 TXT | | 提取证件信息 | 本地 OCR 配合字段规则 | 可编辑字段、复制或导出 TXT | | 把表格图片变成数据 | SLANet 识别结构，结合 OCR 填充文字 | 校正行列与合并单元格，导出 CSV／XLSX | | 把公式图片变成源码 | 本地 LaTeX-OCR | 可编辑 LaTeX、复制或导出 `.tex` | | 阅读外文资料 | Qwen3.5 GGUF + llama.cpp | 在本机翻译 OCR 结果或输入的文字 | | 移除图片背景 | U²-Net、BiRefNet 系列模型 | 保留原尺寸和透明度的图片，可保存 PNG／WebP | | 去水印与图像修复 | MI-GAN、LaMa、Moebius；SLBR 辅助自动检测 | 对照原图检查结果，撤销、复制、保存或贴图 | | 分享前遮盖敏感文字 | 本地 OCR + 规则；可选本地 Qwen 辅助识别人名、地址 | 模糊敏感文字所在范围 | ### 模型大小与识别效果 **识别效果受所选 AI 模型的大小与能力影响。** 对同一系列、同一任务且训练与量化条件相近的模型，较大的参数规模通常有助于提高识别准确率和复杂内容的处理能力；轻量模型则更适合低资源设备和快速处理。OCR、表格、公式和本地翻译分别使用各自的模型，应按任务与设备资源选择兼容模型。 模型越大，内存、显存和处理时间的需求通常也越高。实际效果还取决于模型结构、训练数据、量化方式、语言覆盖及图片清晰度，不能只按下载文件大小判断。对复杂内容，可在兼容范围内选用能力更强的模型，并结合原图检查关键文字、数字和符号。 ### 离线使用如何准备 模型按需配置，不必为了截图一次性下载所有模型。OCR、表格、公式、抠图和本地翻译可在设置中下载配置；去水印页面支持下载或导入对应模型。内置模型下载流程提供来源选择、进度、文件校验与配置，普通使用无需安装 Python 或 CUDA。 如果目标电脑无法联网，先在可联网环境准备程序、所需模型和运行库，再连同本地配置一起部署，并在目标电脑上核对模型路径与设备设置。图像 AI 使用 ONNX Runtime，可选择 CPU 或 DirectML；本地翻译使用独立的 llama.cpp 运行库，可选择 CPU 或 Vulkan。模型越大，对内存、显存和处理时间的要求通常越高。 **本地处理与联网功能分开控制。** 在线翻译和以图搜图默认关闭，启用后每次发送仍需确认。模型下载和更新检查也需要网络；离线 AI 表示推理可脱离互联网运行，不表示程序绝不发起网络请求。历史图片保存在本地，未加密；保存位置、模型管理和数据目录迁移见[配置与依赖](docs/配置与依赖.md)。 [软件介绍](#software) · [快速上手](#start) · [首次配置](#settings) · [文档与开发](#development) ## 软件介绍 启动后，NimCap 截图工具驻留系统托盘，通过快捷键或托盘菜单工作。截图后可以标注、脱敏、复制、保存、贴图，或继续识别。处理已有图片时，先复制图片，按 `Ctrl+Shift+V` 创建贴图，再从贴图右键菜单打开“图像工具”。 下方配图选用仓库已有素材，部分来自更名前的界面或真实 WPF 组件渲染，按钮布局与当前版本可能不同；操作入口以本文和当前程序为准。图像来源与制作方式见[配图说明](Screenshot/Blog/README.md)。 [TRUNCATED]

github.text_excerpt: # liseur-sync Self-hosted server for book libraries and reading-position synchronization. `liseur-sync` is the companion server for [Liseur](https://github.com/chmouel/liseur). It also provides a kosync-compatible API for KOReader and CrossPoint. The server is a single Go binary with SQLite by default, optional PostgreSQL, and multi-user support. Project site: ![Library](docs/screenshots/library.png) ![Insights](docs/screenshots/insights.png) ## Set up KOReader Download the setup from the Devices page, copy its plugin folders into KOReader's `plugins/` folder and start KOReader. The library appears in KOReader's built-in OPDS catalog, reading positions sync through its built-in Progress sync, and reading time goes to the server through the KoInsight plugin, which the setup downloads for you. **[Step-by-step guide with screenshots](https://chmouel.github.io/liseur-sync/koreader/)** ![The Set up KOReader box on the Devices page](docs/site/img/web-setup-card.png) ## Set up CrossPoint On an Xteink running CrossPoint, pair CrossPoint Sync with a code from the Devices page to sync your reading position. Add the OPDS catalog with a library token to download books, and install the statistics plugin the Devices page builds for the reader to record reading time. **[Step-by-step guide with screenshots](https://chmouel.github.io/liseur-sync/crosspoint/)** ## Interfaces `liseur-sync` provides: * reading-position synchronization using full locators * a native REST API * a kosync-compatible API for KOReader and [CrossPoint](docs/crosspoint.md), with paragraph-precise positions shared with Liseur * OPDS 1.2 and OPDS 2.0 catalogs * EPUB library indexing and search * audiobooks found in watched folders, played inside the web reader * EPUB and audiobook upload, and deletion, for writable folders * a browser based EPUB reader that supports offline reading. * per-user reading statistics and sessions * optional [Audiobookshelf chapter and listening sync](docs/deployment.md#following-an-audiobook-on-audiobookshelf) * optional mirroring of an account's positions to another server * per-user series claims * a per-account sentence translation cache. Today, Robota provides composable TypeScript libraries with strict types, multi-provider support, tool calling and a plugin/event architecture. The SDK and maintained interfaces belong to the same environment. `@robota-sdk/agent-cli` delivers a terminal agent with coding capabilities, assembled from the same neutral building blocks you can embed in your own application. > Evaluating with an AI agent? # [Shogo AI](https://shogo.ai) Shogo is an open-source platform for building AI agents that do real work: reading from your systems, taking actions, and running workflows end to end. TypeScript throughout. Self-host it or use Shogo Cloud. **[Website](https://shogo.ai)** · **[Launch Studio](https://studio.shogo.ai)** · **[Documentation](https://shogo.ai/docs)** Shogo combines a Hono API, Expo-based clients, agent runtimes, project runtimes, and a developer SDK into one platform for building and operating agentic products. **License:** the SDK and client libraries you actually integrate (`@shogo-ai/*`, plus the mobile/desktop clients) are MIT. The server components behind Shogo Cloud (`apps/api/`, `packages/agent-runtime/`, `packages/shared-runtime/`) are AGPL-3.0-or-later — a moat against hosted resellers, not a restriction on your own use, modification, or self-hosting. Full breakdown in [Open Source Model](#open-source-model) below and [docs/LICENSING.md](./docs/LICENSING.md). There's no one-command quickstart yet. Running Shogo locally means cloning the repo, installing with Bun, starting Postgres/Redis/MinIO in Docker, and running migrations — realistically a few minutes, not 60 seconds. The real steps are in [Local development](#local-development) below. <!-- coverage-badge:backend --> [![Backend coverage](https://img.shields.io/badge/backend%20coverage-84.30%25-yellow)](./coverage/lcov.info) <!-- /coverage-badge:backend --> <!-- coverage-badge:frontend --> [![Frontend coverage](https://img.shields.io/badge/frontend%20coverage-67.82%25-orange)](./coverage/frontend-lcov.info) <!-- /coverage-badge:frontend --> ## Open Source Model Shogo uses a split-license model. AGPL-3.0-or-later guards the cloud-service surface a competitor would need to ship a hosted clone; everything else is MIT so adoption is friction-free. - AGPL-3.0-or-later: `apps/api/`, `packages/agent-runtime/`, `packages/shared-runtime/` - MIT: the `@shogo-ai/*` libraries, `apps/mobile/`, `apps/desktop/`, `packages/shared-app/`, `packages/shared-ui/`, `packages/ui-kit/`, `packages/domain-stores/`, `templates/runtime-template/` - CC BY 4.0: `apps/docs/`, `docs/` - Proprietary: `terraform/`, `k8s/`, `deploy-examples/`, `.github/workflows/` (see `INFRASTRUCTURE-LICENSE.md`) - The hosted Shogo Cloud offering is proprietary See [docs/LICENSING.md](./docs/LICENSING.md) for the full strategy and ratio
